module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 105

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/105](https://www.erdosproblems.com/105)
- [Be83] Beck, József, *On the lattice property of the plane and some problems of Dirac, Motzkin
  and Erdős in combinatorial geometry*. Combinatorica (1983), 281-297.
- [ErPu95] Erdős, P. and Purdy, G., *Two combinatorial problems in the plane*. Discrete Comput.
  Geom. (1995), 441-443.
- [SzTr83] Szemerédi, Endre and Trotter, Jr., William T., *Extremal problems in discrete
  geometry*. Combinatorica (1983), 381-392.
-/

@[expose] public section

open EuclideanGeometry

namespace Erdos105

/--
Let $A,B\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be disjoint sets of size $n$ and $n-3$ respectively, with not all
of $A$ contained on a single line. Is there a line which contains at least two points from $A$
and no points from $B$?

This has been disproved by Xichuan in the comments, who has found three explicit
counterexamples.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 52, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos105.lean"]
theorem erdos_105 : answer(False) ↔
    ∀ A B : Finset ℝ², Disjoint A B → A.card = B.card + 3 →
      ¬ Collinear ℝ (A : Set ℝ²) →
      ∃ p ∈ A, ∃ q ∈ A, p ≠ q ∧ ∀ b ∈ B, b ∉ line[ℝ, p, q] := by
  sorry

/--
A construction of Hickerson shows that this fails with $n-2$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 52]
theorem erdos_105.variants.hickerson : ¬ ∀ A B : Finset ℝ², Disjoint A B →
    A.card = B.card + 2 → ¬ Collinear ℝ (A : Set ℝ²) →
    ∃ p ∈ A, ∃ q ∈ A, p ≠ q ∧ ∀ b ∈ B, b ∉ line[ℝ, p, q] := by
  sorry

/--
A result independently proved by Beck [Be83] and Szemerédi and Trotter [SzTr83] (see [211])
implies it is true with $n-3$ replaced by $cn$ for some constant $c>0$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 52]
theorem erdos_105.variants.beck_szemeredi_trotter : ∃ c > (0 : ℝ),
    ∀ A B : Finset ℝ², Disjoint A B → (B.card : ℝ) ≤ c * A.card →
      ¬ Collinear ℝ (A : Set ℝ²) →
      ∃ p ∈ A, ∃ q ∈ A, p ≠ q ∧ ∀ b ∈ B, b ∉ line[ℝ, p, q] := by
  sorry

/--
It remains possible that this holds with $n-4$ (or in general with $n-O(1)$ or $(1-o(1))n$).
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 52]
theorem erdos_105.variants.sub_four : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ A B : Finset ℝ², Disjoint A B → A.card = B.card + 4 →
      ¬ Collinear ℝ (A : Set ℝ²) →
      ∃ p ∈ A, ∃ q ∈ A, p ≠ q ∧ ∀ b ∈ B, b ∉ line[ℝ, p, q] := by
  sorry

end Erdos105

status_issues.evidence:
Forum post (http://web.archive.org/web/20260729074345/https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/105, Core_65536, 24 Jul 2026): "I found the following explicit counterexample to the n−4 strengthening mentioned above ... A={(168,0),(280,560),(280,140),(420,630),(360,240),(504,672),(280,-280),(420,0),(840,840),(0,-840)}, B={(0,420),(840,3360),(336,336),(280,0),(420,315),(-840,-2520)}. Thus A∩B=∅, A is not collinear, |A|=10, and |B|=6=|A|−4. Moreover, every line containing at least two points of A contains at least one point of B."

I checked this myself in two ways:
- An exact-integer script confirms all 45 pairs of A are blocked (18 lines; each point of B lies on exactly 3 of them).
- In a Lean scratch file importing `FormalConjectures.ErdosProblems.«105»`, I proved `theorem sub_four_statement_refuted : ¬ type_of% @Erdos105.erdos_105.variants.sub_four` and `False ↔ <the file's RHS>`. `#print axioms` lists only [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]. The proof maps the integer points into ℝ² with `!₂[..]`, uses `decide` for the 45×6 determinant checks, and uses `mem_affineSpan_pair_iff_exists_lineMap_eq` for membership in the line.
status_issues.suggested_change: Replace `answer(sorry)` with `answer(False)` and retag as `@[category research solved, AMS 5 52]`. Update the docstring to cite the counterexample (Core_65536, https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/105, 24 Jul 2026). Keep the n−O(1) and (1−o(1))n questions as open remarks: they are not formalized, and one n−4 counterexample does not settle them.

reformulations.difference: The source says the statement "is true with n−3 replaced by cn for some constant c>0". The Lean writes this as the inequality `(B.card : ℝ) ≤ c * A.card` rather than |B| = cn (cn need not be an integer), and quantifies over all A, not only large ones.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The claim only gets harder as B grows. If B meets every line determined by A, then so does any B' ⊇ B that is disjoint from A, and ℝ² \ A is infinite. So "every B with |B| ≤ cn leaves a line free" is equivalent to "every B with |B| = ⌊cn⌋ leaves a line free". Small n do not matter because c is existentially quantified: if the claim holds for n ≥ N₀ with constant c₀, take c = min(c₀, 1/(N₀+1)). Then for n ≤ N₀ the hypothesis forces B = ∅, and any two distinct points of the non-collinear A give a free line. This is exactly ErPu95's f(n) > C₃n, which follows from Beck's weak-Dirac theorem: some point of A lies on ≥ n/C lines, and each point of B lies on at most one of them.

review.notes:
I checked all four declarations. There are no misformalization findings; the one issue is the stale status of `sub_four`.

**Lean checks** (scratch files /workspace/review/sub_four_counter.lean and /workspace/review/checks2.lean):
- `type_of% @Erdos105.erdos_105` (with the file's `answer(False)`) is provable outright from Xichuan's 12+9 integer configuration, taken from the plby proof.
- `type_of% @Erdos105.erdos_105.variants.hickerson` is provable from the same configuration plus one extra point in B.
- `¬ type_of% @Erdos105.erdos_105.variants.sub_four` is provable from Core_65536's 10+6 configuration.
- All three use only the standard axioms.

**Faithfulness points:**
- `line[ℝ,p,q]` with p ≠ q ∈ A is exactly "a line containing at least two points of A".
- `¬ Collinear ℝ ↑A` is exactly "not all of A on one line", including the empty and small cases.
- `A.card = B.card + 3` agrees with |A| = n, |B| = n−3 whenever n ≥ 3. For |A| < 3 the set A is collinear anyway, so nothing is lost.
- The formal_proof record is consistent: plby's statement (`B.card = n - 3` with truncated subtraction, and "no line contains A") is equivalent to the file's right-hand side.

**Context on the sources:**
- ErPu95 poses the question as "How large is f(n)?", where f(n) is the smallest blocking set for n non-collinear points. It reports f(n) > C₃n (Beck's weak Dirac theorem) and Hickerson's f(n) ≤ n−2 for all n ≥ 6.
- Hickerson's T, and all the forum configurations, use points at infinity. The site states the problem in ℝ², and a projective transformation moving a line that avoids the finite configuration to infinity makes the two versions equivalent. In any case I proved the ℝ² statements directly.
- The Hickerson variant states only that one n−2 counterexample exists. That faithfully renders the site's sentence "fails with n−2", although a stronger "for all n ≥ 6" version would also be accurate.
- The module docstring omits the site's [Er95] reference. This is purely bibliographic.
- I did not read Be83 or SzTr83 themselves. The Beck–Szemerédi–Trotter variant's truth rests on ErPu95's explicit statement and the standard weak-Dirac argument.

I did not modify /opt/formal-conjectures. The `lakefile.toml` change and the untracked `run/` directory are timestamped before my session began.
